root_theorem.statement_nl: Find the minimal value of $k$ such that there exist $k$-by-$k$ real matrices $A_1, \\dots, A_{2025}$ with the property that $A_i A_j = A_j A_i$ if and only if $|i-j| \\in \\{0,1,2024\\}$.

variables.name: k
variables.role: unknown to be minimized; matrix size parameter

variables.name: n
variables.role: number of matrices; shorthand for 2025

variables.name: A_1,...,A_n
variables.domain: A_i \in M_k(\mathbb{R}) (real k-by-k matrices) for each i=1..n
variables.role: witnesses whose pairwise commutation relations are constrained

variables.name: i,j
variables.role: indices ranging over the matrix family used in the commutation condition

quantifier_order: Exist k \in Z_{>0} (we are to choose the minimal such k)
Exists A_1,...,A_n with each A_i \in M_k(R)
For all i,j \in {1,...,n}: (A_i A_j = A_j A_i) iff (|i-j| \in {0,1,n-1})
Minimality clause: for all k' < k, no family A_1',...,A_n' \in M_{k'}(R) satisfies the same iff property
domain_restrictions: k must be a positive integer (matrix dimension)
A_i are k-by-k real matrices (elements of M_k(R))
Indices i,j range over the finite set {1,...,2025}
The absolute difference |i-j| is taken in Z (not modulo) but the set {0,1,2024} is used to encode cyclic adjacency (2024 = n-1)
witness_dependencies: The matrices A_1,...,A_n are existential witnesses depending on the chosen k (i.e. existence quantified after k)
The minimality witness is negative-existence: for all k' < k there do not exist A_1',...,A_n' in M_{k'}(R) with the property
No explicit further dependence of each A_i on i beyond being labeled by index i; the family may be jointly chosen
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let n = 2025. Find the smallest positive integer k such that there exist matrices A_1,...,A_n with A_i \in M_k(R) for all i and such that for every i,j in {1,...,n}, A_i A_j = A_j A_i if and only if |i-j| is in {0,1,n-1}. Equivalently, k = min { k' \in Z_{>0} : there exist A_1,...,A_n in M_{k'}(R) satisfying \forall i,j (A_iA_j = A_jA_i \iff |i-j| \in {0,1,n-1}) }.

selected_decomposition.strategy_summary: Use a corrected lower-bound/upper-bound split, differing from the rejected attempt by replacing the previously under-specified orthogonal-representation lemma with an explicit 3-dimensional construction and by correcting the rank-one commutation criterion to the distinct-index/nonparallel form required by the vetting notes.

steps.trivial_justification: L1 is exactly the negation of existence for k=1.
L4 is exactly the negation of existence for k=2.

steps.derives: There exist 3-by-3 real matrices A_1,\dots,A_{2025} such that for all i,j\in\{1,\dots,2025\}, A_iA_j=A_jA_i if and only if |i-j|\in\{0,1,2024\}.
steps.trivial_justification: L7 states the existence of an explicit family in M_3(R) with the required iff-property.

steps.derives: The minimal value of k such that there exist k-by-k real matrices A_1, \dots, A_{2025} with the property that A_i A_j = A_j A_i if and only if |i-j| \in \{0,1,2024\} is k=3.
steps.trivial_justification: A1 and A2 exclude all positive integers k<3, while A3 gives existence for k=3; therefore the minimum is exactly 3.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: First exclude k=1 by L1. Next exclude k=2 by L4; internally this uses the fact that no A_i can be scalar and that the centralizer of a nonscalar 2-by-2 matrix is commutative, so two neighbors of A_i would incorrectly commute. Then apply L7, which uses the explicit vectors from L5 and the corrected rank-one commutation criterion from L6, to produce a valid family in M_3(R). Since k=3 works and every smaller positive k fails, the minimum is 3.

lemmas.statement_nl: There do not exist real 1-by-1 matrices A_1,\dots,A_{2025} such that for all i,j \in \{1,\dots,2025\}, the equality A_iA_j=A_jA_i holds if and only if |i-j| \in \{0,1,2024\}.

variables.name: A_k
variables.role: existentially quantified indexed family of matrices (the tuple A_1,...,A_2025)

variables.name: i
variables.role: universally quantified index

variables.name: j
variables.role: universally quantified index

domain_restrictions: For each k = 1,...,2025, A_k is a real 1×1 matrix (identifiable with a real number).
i and j range over the finite set {1,...,2025} of integers.
The integer |i-j| takes values in {0,1,...,2024}; the set {0,1,2024} is a subset of that range.
Matrix multiplication and equality refer to the usual real 1×1 matrix (scalar) operations.
witness_dependencies: The existential witnesses are the entire tuple (A_1,...,A_2025) chosen before quantifying over i and j; their values cannot depend on the particular i or j chosen later.
There are no additional existentials whose values may vary with i or j (no i-dependent witnesses).

lemmas.proof_nl:
Assume for contradiction that there exist real 1-by-1 matrices A_1,\dots,A_{2025} such that for all i,j\in\{1,\dots,2025\},
A_iA_j=A_jA_i \iff |i-j|\in\{0,1,2024\}.

A real 1-by-1 matrix is just a real scalar. So for each t there exists a_t\in\mathbb{R} with A_t=[a_t]. Then for any i,j,
A_iA_j=[a_i][a_j]=[a_ia_j]=[a_ja_i]=[a_j][a_i]=A_jA_i,
because multiplication in \mathbb{R} is commutative. Hence A_iA_j=A_jA_i for every pair i,j\in\{1,\dots,2025\}.

Now take i=1 and j=3. Then A_1A_3=A_3A_1, but |1-3|=2, and 2\notin\{0,1,2024\}. This contradicts the assumed equivalence.

Therefore no such family of real 1-by-1 matrices exists.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let B be a 2-by-2 real matrix that is not a scalar multiple of the identity matrix I_2. Then every 2-by-2 real matrix X satisfying XB=BX can be written uniquely in the form X=\alpha I_2+\beta B with real numbers \alpha,\beta. In particular, any two 2-by-2 real matrices commuting with B also commute with each other.

variables.name: B
variables.role: parameter; fixed matrix that is assumed not to be a scalar multiple of the identity

variables.name: I_2
variables.role: the 2x2 identity matrix (constant)

variables.name: X
variables.role: arbitrary matrix under the hypothesis that it commutes with B (i.e. XB = BX)

variables.name: alpha
variables.role: existential witness (coefficient of I_2) depending on X and B

variables.name: beta
variables.role: existential witness (coefficient of B) depending on X and B

quantifier_order: For all B in M_2(R) with (not exists lambda in R such that B = lambda * I_2)
For all X in M_2(R) with XB = BX
There exist unique alpha, beta in R such that X = alpha * I_2 + beta * B
Consequently: For all X,Y in M_2(R) with XB = BX and YB = BY, XY = YX
domain_restrictions: B ∈ M_2(R) (the set of 2x2 real matrices)
B is NOT a scalar multiple of I_2: ¬∃λ ∈ R with B = λ I_2
X ∈ M_2(R) and satisfies the commutation relation XB = BX
alpha, beta ∈ R (real numbers)
Matrix multiplication and equality are over the real field
witness_dependencies: alpha and beta are functions of (X,B); i.e. for each fixed B (satisfying the hypothesis) and each X with XB=BX there is a uniquely determined pair (alpha,beta)
Uniqueness relies on I_2 and B being R-linearly independent (which follows from the hypothesis B ≠ λ I_2)
The 'in particular' witness-free claim (commutativity of any two elements of the centralizer) follows because all commuting X are polynomials in B (degree ≤1), so multiplication is commutative
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every B ∈ M_2(R) with ¬∃λ ∈ R such that B = λ I_2, the centralizer C(B) = {X ∈ M_2(R) : XB = BX} equals {α I_2 + β B : α,β ∈ R}. Equivalently, ∀B (B ∈ M_2(R) and B ≠ λ I_2 for any λ ∈ R) ⇒ (∀X ∈ M_2(R), XB = BX ⇔ ∃!α,β ∈ R with X = α I_2 + β B). Consequently, for such B, any X,Y ∈ M_2(R) with XB = BX and YB = BY satisfy XY = YX.

lemmas.proof_nl:
View B as a linear endomorphism of V = R^2. First I claim there exists v in V such that v and Bv are linearly independent. Suppose not. Then for every nonzero u in V we have Bu in span(u), so every nonzero vector is an eigenvector of B. Choose a basis e1, e2 of V. Then Be1 = lambda1 e1 and Be2 = lambda2 e2 for some real lambda1, lambda2. Also e1 + e2 is nonzero, so B(e1 + e2) = mu(e1 + e2) for some mu in R. But B(e1 + e2) = lambda1 e1 + lambda2 e2, and since e1, e2 are linearly independent, this forces lambda1 = mu = lambda2. Hence B = lambda1 I_2, contradicting the hypothesis that B is not a scalar multiple of I_2. Therefore there exists v with {v, Bv} linearly independent; because dim V = 2, this set is a basis of V.

Now let X in M_2(R) satisfy XB = BX. Since {v, Bv} is a basis, there exist unique real numbers alpha, beta such that Xv = alpha v + beta Bv. Set T := alpha I_2 + beta B. Then Tv = alpha v + beta Bv = Xv. Also, using XB = BX, we get X(Bv) = B(Xv) = B(alpha v + beta Bv) = alpha Bv + beta B^2 v. On the other hand, T(Bv) = alpha Bv + beta B(Bv) = alpha Bv + beta B^2 v. So T(Bv) = X(Bv) as well. Thus X and T agree on the basis {v, Bv}, hence X = T. Therefore X = alpha I_2 + beta B.

The representation is unique: if alpha I_2 + beta B = alpha' I_2 + beta' B, then applying both sides to v gives (alpha - alpha')v + (beta - beta')Bv = 0. Since v and Bv are linearly independent, alpha = alpha' and beta = beta'.

Conversely, every matrix of the form alpha I_2 + beta B commutes with B, because (alpha I_2 + beta B)B = alpha B + beta B^2 = B(alpha I_2 + beta B). Hence the centralizer of B is exactly {alpha I_2 + beta B : alpha, beta in R}.

Finally, if X and Y both commute with B, then X = alpha I_2 + beta B and Y = gamma I_2 + delta B for some real alpha, beta, gamma, delta. Therefore XY = (alpha I_2 + beta B)(gamma I_2 + delta B) = agamma I_2 + (adelta + bgamma)B + bdelta B^2 = (gamma I_2 + delta B)(alpha I_2 + beta B) = YX. So any two 2-by-2 real matrices commuting with B also commute with each other.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Provides the key structural fact about centralizers in M_2(R).

lemmas.statement_nl: Suppose A_1,\dots,A_{2025} are 2-by-2 real matrices such that for all i,j \in \{1,\dots,2025\}, one has A_iA_j=A_jA_i if and only if |i-j| \in \{0,1,2024\}. Then no A_i is a scalar multiple of the identity matrix I_2.

variables.name: A_1,...,A_2025
variables.domain: M_2(R)^{2025} (each A_k is a 2x2 real matrix)
variables.role: given family of matrices, universally quantified as a hypothesis subject to the commutation condition

variables.name: i
variables.role: index ranging over the matrices (used in universal quantifiers in the hypothesis and conclusion)

variables.name: j
variables.role: index ranging over the matrices (used in the hypothesis)

variables.name: \lambda
variables.role: candidate scalar for 'scalar multiple of identity' (appears in the existential negation in the conclusion)

variables.name: I_2
variables.role: the 2x2 identity matrix; canonical constant

quantifier_order: For all tuples (A_1,...,A_2025) in M_2(R)^{2025}:
assume (Hypothesis) for all i,j in {1,...,2025} (ordered pairs), (A_i A_j = A_j A_i) if and only if (|i-j| in {0,1,2024});
conclude (Claim) for all i in {1,...,2025}, there does NOT exist a real \lambda such that A_i = \lambda I_2.
domain_restrictions: Each A_k is a 2x2 matrix with real entries (A_k ∈ M_2(R)).
Indices i,j are integers in the finite set {1,...,2025}.
"|i-j|" is the usual absolute difference on integers (so |i-j|=2024 means pairs with indices differing by 2024, i.e. the pair (1,2025) etc.).
Scalars \lambda are real numbers (\lambda ∈ R).
Matrix multiplication is the usual real 2x2 matrix multiplication; I_2 is the 2x2 identity.
witness_dependencies: Any existential witness \lambda_i (asserting A_i = \lambda_i I_2) would be allowed to depend on the index i. (In formal terms the forbidden statement is: there exists i in {1..2025} and exists \lambda in R such that A_i = \lambda I_2.)
No existential witness is claimed in the hypothesis; the hypothesis is a universal biconditional over ordered pairs (i,j).

The commutation relation is global: whether A_i commutes with A_j may depend on both i and j and on the entire tuple (A_1,...,A_2025), but any single-scalar witness for A_i depends only on i (and trivially on the matrix A_i itself).
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every tuple (A_1,...,A_2025) of 2x2 real matrices satisfying ∀i,j ∈ {1,..,2025}: (A_i A_j = A_j A_i) ⇔ (|i-j| ∈ {0,1,2024}), we have ∀i ∈ {1,..,2025}, ∀λ ∈ R: A_i ≠ λ I_2. Equivalently, there does not exist an index i and a real scalar λ with A_i = λ I_2.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Assume for contradiction that there exists an index i\in\{1,\dots,2025\} and a real number \lambda such that A_i=\lambda I_2.

We first choose an index j\in\{1,\dots,2025\} which is not equal to i and is not cyclically adjacent to i in the sense of the set \{0,1,2024\}. Such a j always exists:
- if 1\le i\le 2023, take j=i+2; then |i-j|=2,
- if i=2024, take j=2021; then |i-j|=3,
- if i=2025, take j=2022; then |i-j|=3.
In every case, j\in\{1,\dots,2025\} and |i-j|\notin\{0,1,2024\}.

Now, since A_i=\lambda I_2, we have
A_iA_j=(\lambda I_2)A_j=\lambda A_j=A_j(\lambda I_2)=A_jA_i.
So A_i and A_j commute.

But the hypothesis says that for all indices p,q\in\{1,\dots,2025\},
A_pA_q=A_qA_p \iff |p-q|\in\{0,1,2024\}.
Applying this with p=i and q=j, the fact that A_i and A_j commute implies
|i-j|\in\{0,1,2024\}.
This contradicts the choice of j.

Therefore no such i and \lambda can exist. Hence for every i\in\{1,\dots,2025\}, the matrix A_i is not a scalar multiple of the identity matrix I_2.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Ensures L2 applies to every A_i in a hypothetical k=2 realization.

lemmas.statement_nl: There do not exist 2-by-2 real matrices A_1,\dots,A_{2025} such that for all i,j \in \{1,\dots,2025\}, the equality A_iA_j=A_jA_i holds if and only if |i-j| \in \{0,1,2024\}.

variables.name: A_1,...,A_{2025}
variables.domain: M_2(\mathbb{R})^ {2025} (each A_k is a 2x2 real matrix)
variables.role: existentially quantified family of matrices (the claimed nonexistent witness)

variables.name: i
variables.role: first universal index

variables.name: j
variables.role: second universal index

quantifier_order: not (exists A_1,...,A_{2025} in M_2(R))
for all i in {1,...,2025}
for all j in {1,...,2025}
domain_restrictions: Each A_k is an arbitrary 2x2 matrix with real entries (no further constraints like invertibility or distinctness are given).
i and j range over the finite set of integers {1,...,2025}.
Matrix multiplication and equality are the standard operations on M_2(R).
Absolute difference |i-j| is the usual integer absolute value (not modular arithmetic), so |1-2025| = 2024, which makes the pair (1,2025) an 'adjacent' pair in the stated condition.
witness_dependencies: The existential quantifier (if it were true) ranges over a single global tuple (A_1,...,A_{2025}) that does not depend on i or j; i and j are only universally quantified afterwards.
Because the statement negates the existence, there is asserted to be no such global tuple of matrices.

The iff condition imposes two requirements simultaneously: (a) for any i,j with |i-j| in {0,1,2024}, A_i and A_j must commute; (b) for any i,j with |i-j| not in {0,1,2024}, A_i and A_j must not commute. Both directions must hold for the same global tuple.
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: ¬∃(A_1,...,A_{2025} ∈ M_2(R)) such that ∀i,j ∈ {1,...,2025}, [A_i A_j = A_j A_i ⇔ |i-j| ∈ {0,1,2024}]. Equivalently: For every tuple (A_1,...,A_{2025}) of 2x2 real matrices, ∃ i,j ∈ {1,...,2025} with (A_i A_j = A_j A_i) xor (|i-j| ∈ {0,1,2024}) (i.e. the commutation relation does not equal the predicate |i-j|∈{0,1,2024}).

lemmas.proof_nl:
Assume for contradiction that there exist matrices A_1,\dots,A_{2025} in M_2(\mathbb R) such that for all i,j\in\{1,\dots,2025\},
A_iA_j=A_jA_i \iff |i-j|\in\{0,1,2024\}.

First note that A_2 is not a scalar matrix. Indeed, if A_2=\lambda I for some \lambda\in\mathbb R, then A_2 would commute with every 2\times 2 real matrix, in particular with A_4. But |2-4|=2, and 2\notin\{0,1,2024\}, so by the required property A_2 and A_4 should not commute. Contradiction.

Now we prove the following general fact.

Claim: If A\in M_2(\mathbb R) is non-scalar, then any two matrices in M_2(\mathbb R) that commute with A also commute with each other.

Proof of claim: Since A is non-scalar, there exists a vector v\in\mathbb R^2 such that v and Av are linearly independent. Indeed, if for every v we had Av\in \mathbb R v, then every nonzero vector would be an eigenvector of A. Applying this to the standard basis vectors e_1,e_2 gives Ae_1=\lambda e_1 and Ae_2=\mu e_2 for some \lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R. Then A(e_1+e_2) must also lie in the line \mathbb R(e_1+e_2), but
A(e_1+e_2)=\lambda e_1+\mu e_2,
so necessarily \lambda=\mu. Hence A=\lambda I, contradicting that A is non-scalar. Therefore such a vector v exists.

So (v,Av) is a basis of \mathbb R^2. Write
A^2v=pv+qAv
for some real numbers p,q.

Let B be any matrix commuting with A. Since (v,Av) is a basis, there exist unique x,y\in\mathbb R such that
Bv=xv+yAv.
Because BA=AB,
B(Av)=A(Bv)=A(xv+yAv)=xAv+yA^2v=yp\,v+(x+yq)Av.
Now consider the matrix xI+yA. It satisfies
(xI+yA)v=xv+yAv,
and
(xI+yA)(Av)=xAv+yA^2v=yp\,v+(x+yq)Av.
Thus B and xI+yA agree on the basis vectors v and Av, so B=xI+yA.

Hence every matrix commuting with A has the form xI+yA. Therefore if C also commutes with A, say C=uI+wA, then
BC=(xI+yA)(uI+wA)=(uI+wA)(xI+yA)=CB,
because both are polynomials in A. This proves the claim.

Apply the claim with A=A_2. We already know A_2 is non-scalar. Also, by the given condition,
A_1A_2=A_2A_1 because |1-2|=1,
and
A_3A_2=A_2A_3 because |3-2|=1.
So both A_1 and A_3 commute with A_2. By the claim, A_1 and A_3 commute with each other.

But |1-3|=2, and 2\notin\{0,1,2024\}. Therefore the required property says A_1 and A_3 must not commute. This contradiction shows that no such family A_1,\dots,A_{2025} exists.

Therefore there do not exist 2-by-2 real matrices A_1,\dots,A_{2025} satisfying the stated condition.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Excludes k=2 by combining L2 and L3 internally.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n=2025, let m=1012, let \theta = 2\pi m/n = \pi-\pi/2025, and let c=\sqrt{-\cos\theta}. For each i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, define a vector v_i\in\mathbb R^3 by v_i=(\cos(i\theta),\sin(i\theta),c). Then for any distinct i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}, one has v_i\cdot v_j=0 if and only if |i-j|\in\{1,n-1\}, and moreover v_i and v_j are not parallel.

variables.name: n
variables.role: fixed parameter (number of vectors, period denominator)

variables.name: m
variables.role: fixed parameter (numerator in angle fraction)

variables.name: theta
variables.role: common angular step; used in coordinates cos(i theta), sin(i theta)

variables.name: c
variables.domain: c = sqrt(-cos(theta)) \in R_{\ge 0}; in fact cos(theta) < 0 so c > 0
variables.role: third-coordinate common constant; ensures v_i nonzero

variables.name: i
variables.role: index for family of vectors v_i

variables.name: j
variables.role: second index for pair of vectors v_i, v_j

variables.name: v_i
variables.domain: v_i = (cos(i theta), sin(i theta), c) \in R^3, for each i
variables.role: family of vectors whose pairwise relations are claimed

variables.name: k
variables.role: difference of indices used to reduce dot-product condition

quantifier_order: n = 2025 fixed
m = 1012 fixed
theta defined as 2π m / n
c defined as sqrt(-cos theta)
for each i in {1,...,n} define v_i in R^3
for all distinct i,j in {1,...,n} assert the following equivalence and additional non-parallel claim
domain_restrictions: n is the integer 2025 (>0)
m is the integer 1012
theta = 2π m / n is a real multiple of 2π with denominator n
cos(theta) < 0 so -cos(theta) > 0 and c = sqrt(-cos(theta)) is defined and positive (convention: principal/nonnegative square root)
indices i,j range over integers 1..n and are distinct when the pairwise claim is made
v_i are nonzero vectors because c > 0 (third coordinate nonzero)
witness_dependencies: To deduce orthogonality: v_i · v_j = cos((i-j) theta) + c^2 = 0, using c^2 = -cos(theta). Thus cos((i-j) theta) = cos(theta). From cos(A) = cos(B) there exists t ∈ Z and choice of sign s ∈ {+1,-1} with (i-j) theta = s theta + 2π t. The integer t (and choice s) depends on i and j.

Converting (i-j) theta = s theta + 2π t to an integer congruence yields (i-j - s) m = t n. The existence of integer t witnessing this equation depends on i,j and on m,n; using gcd(m,n)=1 (see implicit assumptions) one deduces i-j ≡ s (mod n). Thus the witness t depends on (i,j,s) but is eliminated by the gcd argument.

For the non-parallel claim: a hypothetical scalar λ with v_i = λ v_j would satisfy c = λ c, so λ = 1; that 'witness' λ is forced to be 1 and then i=j, contradicting distinctness. Thus no nontrivial scalar witness exists for distinct indices.
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Given fixed integers n=2025 and m=1012, theta = 2π m / n and c = sqrt(-cos(theta)) > 0, define v_i = (cos(i theta), sin(i theta), c) in R^3 for i in {1,...,n}. Then for all distinct i,j in {1,...,n}: (v_i · v_j = 0) if and only if |i - j| ∈ {1, n-1}; furthermore for all distinct i,j the vectors v_i and v_j are not scalar multiples of each other (i.e. not parallel).

lemmas.proof_nl:
First, 0<π/2025<π/2, so cos(π/2025)>0. Because θ=π-π/2025, we have cos θ = -cos(π/2025)<0. Hence c=sqrt(-cos θ)>0, so every v_i is nonzero.

Fix distinct i,j and write d=i-j. Then d≠0 and |d|≤n-1=2024. Using cos x cos y + sin x sin y = cos(x-y),
 v_i·v_j = cos(iθ)cos(jθ)+sin(iθ)sin(jθ)+c^2 = cos((i-j)θ)+c^2 = cos(dθ)-cos θ,
because c^2=-cos θ. Therefore v_i·v_j=0 iff cos(dθ)=cos θ.

Assume v_i·v_j=0. Then cos(dθ)=cos θ. Since cos x - cos y = -2 sin((x+y)/2) sin((x-y)/2), the equality cos x=cos y is equivalent to x=2πt+y or x=2πt-y for some t in Z. Applying this with x=dθ and y=θ, either dθ=2πt+θ or dθ=2πt-θ. As θ=2πm/n with m=1012 and n=2025, these become either m(d-1)=tn or m(d+1)=tn. Now gcd(m,n)=gcd(1012,2025)=1, because 2025=2*1012+1. So n divides d-1 or d+1; equivalently d≡1 or d≡-1 mod n.
Because -(n-1)≤d≤n-1 and d≠0, the congruence d≡1 mod n gives d=1 or d=-(n-1), while d≡-1 mod n gives d=-1 or d=n-1. Hence |d|∈{1,n-1}, i.e. |i-j|∈{1,n-1}.

Conversely, if |i-j|=1, then d=±1, so cos(dθ)=cos θ and thus v_i·v_j=0. If |i-j|=n-1, then d=±(n-1). Since nθ=2πm, we get
 cos((n-1)θ)=cos(nθ-θ)=cos(2πm-θ)=cos θ,
and also cos(-(n-1)θ)=cos((n-1)θ). Thus again v_i·v_j=0. Therefore, for distinct i,j,
 v_i·v_j=0 iff |i-j|∈{1,n-1}.

Now suppose distinct v_i and v_j were parallel. Then v_i=λv_j for some real λ. Comparing third coordinates gives c=λc. Since c>0, λ=1, so actually v_i=v_j. Thus cos(iθ)=cos(jθ) and sin(iθ)=sin(jθ). Therefore
 cos((i-j)θ)=cos(iθ)cos(jθ)+sin(iθ)sin(jθ)=1.
For real x, cos x=1 iff x=2πt for some t in Z. Hence (i-j)θ=2πt for some t in Z. Substituting θ=2πm/n gives (i-j)m=tn. Again gcd(m,n)=1, so n divides i-j. But |i-j|≤n-1, hence i-j=0, so i=j, contradicting distinctness. Therefore no two distinct vectors v_i and v_j are parallel.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Supplies an explicit 3-dimensional configuration encoding the 2025-cycle by orthogonality and fixes the earlier missing-construction issue.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let u,v\in\mathbb R^3 be nonzero vectors that are not parallel. Define rank-one symmetric matrices A=uu^{\mathsf T} and B=vv^{\mathsf T} in M_3(\mathbb R). Then AB=BA if and only if u\cdot v=0. Also, for every such A, one has AA=AA, so each matrix commutes with itself automatically.

variables.name: u
variables.role: first given nonzero vector; used to define A = u u^T

variables.name: v
variables.role: second given nonzero vector, assumed not parallel to u; used to define B = v v^T

variables.name: A
variables.role: rank-one symmetric matrix defined as A = u u^T

variables.name: B
variables.role: rank-one symmetric matrix defined as B = v v^T

quantifier_order: forall u in R^3 \ {0}
forall v in R^3 \ {0} such that v is not parallel to u
define A := u u^T in M_3(R) and B := v v^T in M_3(R)
claim: (A B = B A) iff (u \cdot v = 0)
separately: forall u in R^3 \ {0}, with A := u u^T, A commutes with itself (A A = A A)
domain_restrictions: u and v are nonzero vectors (u != 0, v != 0)
v is not parallel to u (i.e. there is no scalar \lambda with v = \lambda u)
A and B are defined as rank-one symmetric matrices A = u u^T, B = v v^T in M_3(R)
inner product u \cdot v is the standard Euclidean dot product on R^3
matrix multiplication and equality are in M_3(R)
witness_dependencies: A is defined from u (A depends on u): A = u u^T
B is defined from v (B depends on v): B = v v^T
no existential witnesses appear in the main equivalence; the claim is universal
the equivalence conclusion uses the nonparallel assumption to rule out the alternative (u \cdot v != 0 and u,v parallel)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all u,v in R^3 with u != 0, v != 0, and v not parallel to u, let A := u u^T and B := v v^T in M_3(R). Then A B = B A if and only if u \cdot v = 0. Additionally, for all u != 0 in R^3, with A := u u^T, the identity A A = A A holds (i.e. A commutes with itself, a trivial tautology).

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let c := u^T v = u·v. Since c is a scalar,
AB = (u u^T)(v v^T) = u(u^T v)v^T = c u v^T,
and similarly
BA = (v v^T)(u u^T) = v(v^T u)u^T = c v u^T,
because v^T u = u^T v = c.

If u·v = 0, then c = 0, so AB = 0 and BA = 0. Hence AB = BA.

Conversely, assume AB = BA. If c = 0, then already u·v = 0, so there is nothing to prove. Suppose instead that c != 0. Then from c u v^T = c v u^T we may divide by c and obtain
u v^T = v u^T.
Because u != 0, at least one coordinate u_j is nonzero for some j in {1,2,3}. Compare the j-th columns of the two sides. The j-th column of u v^T is v_j u, while the j-th column of v u^T is u_j v. Therefore
v_j u = u_j v.
Since u_j != 0, this implies v = (v_j/u_j)u. Thus v is a scalar multiple of u, i.e. v is parallel to u, contradicting the hypothesis that u and v are not parallel. Hence the case c != 0 is impossible, so c = 0. Therefore u·v = 0.

Thus AB = BA if and only if u·v = 0.

For the second statement, for any nonzero u and A = u u^T, the equality AA = AA is true by reflexivity of equality. Hence every such A commutes with itself automatically.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Corrected version of the previously faulty rank-one criterion; used to convert orthogonality data into the exact commuting relation.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let n=2025, let m=1012, let \theta = 2\pi m/n, let c=\sqrt{-\cos\theta}, and for each i\in\{1,\dots,n\} define v_i=(\cos(i\theta),\sin(i\theta),c)\in\mathbb R^3 and A_i=v_i v_i^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R). Then for all i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}, the equality A_iA_j=A_jA_i holds if and only if |i-j|\in\{0,1,2024\}.

variables.name: n
variables.role: fixed constant (problem parameter)

variables.name: m
variables.role: fixed constant (problem parameter)

variables.name: θ
variables.role: defined constant (depends on n,m)

variables.name: c
variables.role: defined constant (depends on θ)

variables.name: i
variables.role: universally quantified index

variables.name: j
variables.role: universally quantified index

variables.name: v_i
variables.domain: v_i = (cos(iθ), sin(iθ), c) ∈ R^3 (taken as a column vector)
variables.role: derived object depending on i,θ,c

variables.name: A_i
variables.domain: A_i = v_i v_i^T ∈ M_3(R) (outer product, symmetric rank ≤ 1)
variables.role: derived object depending on v_i

quantifier_order: n and m are fixed first: n = 2025, m = 1012
θ is defined next: θ = 2π m / n (real)
c is defined next: c = sqrt(-cos θ) (real, requires -cos θ ≥ 0)
for all i ∈ {1,...,n} (integer index)
for all j ∈ {1,...,n} (integer index)
statement about A_i and A_j (matrices in M_3(R))
domain_restrictions: n and m are integers with n = 2025, m = 1012 (so m < n)
θ ∈ R defined by rational multiple of 2π; in particular θ = 2π * 1012 / 2025
c is real and requires -cos θ ≥ 0 so that the square root is real (take principal sqrt ≥ 0)
i and j range over the integer set {1,...,n}
v_i is a real 3-vector (column) with first two coordinates cos(iθ), sin(iθ) and third coordinate c
A_i denotes the outer product v_i v_i^T, a real 3×3 matrix
witness_dependencies: θ depends on (n,m): θ = 2π m / n
c depends on θ: c = sqrt(-cos θ)
v_i depends on i, θ, c: v_i = (cos(iθ), sin(iθ), c)
A_i depends on v_i: A_i = v_i v_i^T
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For the fixed integers n = 2025 and m = 1012, with θ = 2π m / n and c = sqrt(-cos θ) (real), and with v_i and A_i defined as above, the following holds: ∀ i,j ∈ {1,...,n}, A_i A_j = A_j A_i ⇔ |i - j| ∈ {0,1,2024}. Here |i-j| denotes the ordinary integer absolute difference (taking values in {0,1,...,2024}).

lemmas.proof_nl:
Since theta = 2*pi*1012/2025 = pi - pi/2025, we have cos(theta) = -cos(pi/2025) < 0. Hence c = sqrt(-cos(theta)) > 0, so each v_i is nonzero.

Fix i,j and let d = |i-j|. Put s = v_i^T v_j. Using cos x cos y + sin x sin y = cos(x-y) and c^2 = -cos(theta),
s = cos(i theta) cos(j theta) + sin(i theta) sin(j theta) + c^2
  = cos((i-j)theta) - cos(theta)
  = cos(d theta) - cos(theta),
because cosine is even.

Also,
A_i A_j = (v_i v_i^T)(v_j v_j^T) = v_i(v_i^T v_j)v_j^T = s v_i v_j^T,
A_j A_i = s v_j v_i^T.

Assume first that A_i A_j = A_j A_i.

If s = 0, then cos(d theta) = cos(theta). Since theta = 2*pi*m/n with m = 1012, n = 2025, and gcd(m,n) = 1, the criterion cos x = cos y iff x-y or x+y is an integer multiple of 2*pi gives md ≡ m or md ≡ -m (mod n). Because gcd(m,n) = 1, we may cancel m modulo n, so d ≡ 1 or d ≡ -1 (mod n). As 0 <= d <= n-1 = 2024, this yields d in {1,2024}.

If s != 0, then from s v_i v_j^T = s v_j v_i^T we get v_i v_j^T = v_j v_i^T. Multiply on the right by v_i:
(v_i v_j^T) v_i = (v_j v_i^T) v_i,
so s v_i = (v_i^T v_i) v_j.
Because v_i^T v_i > 0, this shows v_j is a scalar multiple of v_i. But both vectors have third coordinate c > 0, so the scalar is 1 and hence v_j = v_i. Therefore
(cos(i theta), sin(i theta)) = (cos(j theta), sin(j theta)).
Taking the dot product of these two unit vectors, we get
1 = cos(i theta) cos(j theta) + sin(i theta) sin(j theta) = cos((i-j)theta).
Hence (i-j)theta is an integer multiple of 2*pi. Since theta = 2*pi*m/n, this means n divides (i-j)m. Because gcd(m,n) = 1, n divides i-j. But i,j are in {1,...,n}, so |i-j| <= n-1. Therefore i = j, i.e. d = 0.

Thus A_i A_j = A_j A_i implies d in {0,1,2024}.

Conversely, if d = 0 then i = j, so A_i A_j = A_i^2 = A_j A_i.
If d = 1, then s = cos(theta) - cos(theta) = 0, hence A_i A_j = A_j A_i = 0.
If d = 2024 = n-1, then d ≡ -1 (mod n), so d theta ≡ -theta (mod 2*pi); hence cos(d theta) = cos(theta), so again s = 0 and A_i A_j = A_j A_i = 0.

Therefore A_i A_j = A_j A_i if and only if |i-j| is in {0,1,2024}, exactly as claimed.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Establishes the upper bound k\le 3 with explicit witnesses.
